extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and practicing picture-book authors / children's writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on techniques and structural choices that encourage readers to flip to the next spread in picture books, plus procedural steps (read widely, make a dummy) to develop that skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong story that propels action forward
rubrics_metrics.description: Above all, a strong story will do the trick, a story that contains elements that propel action forward.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post lists concrete story structures that create page turns: a trip (readers want to know the journey's end — e.g., LAST STOP ON MARKET STREET), a quest (will they find something spectacular — e.g., SAM AND DAVE DIG A HOLE), strong cause-and-effect (suspense about physical consequences — e.g., THE CAT IN THE HAT), and an escalating problem (each turn raises stakes — e.g., THERE WAS AN OLD DRAGON WHO SWALLOWED A KNIGHT). Use these story-driving elements to create forward momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of questions
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of questions forces readers to look for answers on the next page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonfiction and concept books can pose a question on one spread that requires turning to the next spread to learn the answer — example: WHAT DO YOU DO WITH A TAIL LIKE THIS? This is an active device to compel page turns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rhyme (use with caution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rhyme can encourage readers to guess a missing end rhyme and then turn the page to confirm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhyme creates anticipatory momentum, but the author warns: only write in rhyme if your story demands it and you work diligently to make all the elements of rhyme work. There is a linked post on writing rhyme for more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sparse text to increase pace
rubrics_metrics.description: Sparse text causes readers to move quickly through spreads to add to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Very short text (example: YO! YES? by Chris Raschka) speeds reading and encourages forward movement. Sparse text can be paired with other devices (e.g., alternating characters or strong visuals) to sustain interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Alternating between two balanced characters keeps readers turning pages to see what the other character is doing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two characters are fairly balanced in importance and appearance, the interplay (turn-taking) creates momentum — example: HERMAN AND ROSIE. This technique works especially well with sparse text or dialog-driven spreads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Page-turning words and ellipsis
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'page-turning word' (like 'then') and/or an ellipsis can require a page turn to complete a sentence or idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a connective or trailing punctuation at the end of a spread signals continuation and invites the reader to flip the page to finish the thought — example: ALL YOU NEED FOR A SNOWMAN uses 'then' followed by an ellipsis to force a turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop an internal rhythm / feel for page breaks
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors develop a subconscious rhythm for where page turns occur; writers can develop the same feel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because editors mentally break texts into spreads as they read, writers should train themselves to feel natural points for page breaks. Practicing by reading widely and making dummies helps build this internal rhythm so page turns feel organic rather than forced.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read lots of picture books
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to many picture books trains your sense of pacing, where page turns work, and what techniques different books use. Reading is presented as the foundational practice for learning page-turn craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a dummy of your picture book text
rubrics_metrics.description: #2 MAKE A DUMMY OF YOUR PICTURE BOOK TEXT
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creating a physical or digital dummy of your manuscript helps you visualize spreads, test page-turn points, and see pacing. The post notes there is a separate how-to post for making dummies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intentionally incorporate elements to encourage page turns
rubrics_metrics.description: #3 INCORPORATE ELEMENTS TO ENCOURAGE PAGE TURNS
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a catch-all directive: consciously use story structures, questions, rhyme (when appropriate), sparse text, alternating characters, page-turning words/ellipsis, and other techniques from the post to design page turns rather than leaving them to chance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Think visually; aim for short, deep, subtle, original text and a strong last sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Eve Bunting's advice (quoted in comments): 'Think visually, short, deep, subtle, original, and the last sentence needs to be the best one, leaving the child with hope of some kind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance emphasizes visual storytelling, economy of language, emotional depth/subtlety, originality, and an ending line that provides hope — all of which support meaningful page turns and satisfying read-through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use illustration subplots / hidden elements to create dramatic irony
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot running through the illustrations (a secret the reader sees but the character doesn't) keeps readers turning pages to see when/if the main character will discover it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example from comments: No Yeti Yet uses an illustrative subplot that gives the reader privileged information and compels page turns to watch for discovery. Plan illustrations to carry parallel action or secrets that reward page turns.
